notes.definition: Flame tests identify some metal ions (cations) from the colour they give to a flame: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red and copper green.
explanation: When compounds of certain metals are heated strongly in a flame, the metal ions give out light of a characteristic colour. This makes the flame test a quick way to identify the metal ion in an unknown compound. AQA requires you to know five colours: lithium ions (Li⁺) give a crimson flame, sodium ions (Na⁺) yellow, potassium ions (K⁺) lilac, calcium ions (Ca²⁺) orange-red and copper(II) ions (Cu²⁺) green.

To carry out a flame test, first clean a nichrome wire loop by dipping it in dilute hydrochloric acid and holding it in a hot Bunsen flame until it gives no colour. Then dip the clean loop in the acid and into the solid sample so that a little sticks to it. Hold the loop in the edge of a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame, which is hot and has almost no colour of its own, and observe the colour. Clean the loop again between samples so that one sample does not contaminate the next. This is part of required practical 7 (identifying ions).

The test works best when the sample contains a single metal ion. If a sample contains a mixture of ions, some flame colours can be masked (hidden) by others. Sodium is the classic example: its intense yellow colour can hide the lilac of potassium, so a mixture of sodium and potassium compounds usually just looks yellow. Even small traces of sodium contamination can give a yellow tinge, which is why the loop must be cleaned well.

Flame tests identify the metal ion only; they tell you nothing about the negative ion. Lithium chloride and lithium carbonate both give a crimson flame. To identify the whole compound, flame tests are combined with tests for negative ions, such as adding dilute acid to test for carbonates or silver nitrate solution to test for halides. Some metal ions, such as magnesium and aluminium, give no distinctive flame colour, so they are identified using sodium hydroxide solution instead.
keyFacts: Use a nichrome wire loop cleaned in dilute hydrochloric acid, and a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame.
In a mixture of ions, some flame colours can be masked, for example sodium's yellow hides potassium's lilac.
Flame tests identify the metal ion, not the negative ion.

keyTerms.definition: A test in which a sample is held in a hot flame and the colour produced is used to identify the metal ion.
A positive ion, such as a metal ion like Na⁺ or Ca²⁺.
An unreactive metal wire loop used to hold the sample in the flame; it gives no flame colour of its own.
A blue Bunsen flame with the air hole open; it is very hot and nearly colourless.
When the flame colour of one ion hides the colour of another in a mixture.
A deep red colour; the flame colour of lithium ions.

workedExamples.title: Identifying an ion from a flame colour
workedExamples.question: A white solid gives a lilac flame. Which metal ion does it contain?
steps: Recall the five AQA flame colours: Li⁺ crimson, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Cu²⁺ green.

workedExamples.title: Explaining an unexpected result
workedExamples.question: A student tests a sample known to contain potassium chloride, but the flame is yellow. Suggest two explanations.
steps: Yellow is the flame colour of sodium ions.
The sample may also contain sodium ions, which mask the lilac of potassium.
Or the loop was not cleaned properly and was contaminated with a sodium compound from a previous test.
workedExamples.answer: Sodium ions present in the sample mask the lilac colour, or the wire loop was contaminated with sodium.

workedExamples.title: Distinguishing two red flames
workedExamples.question: Two samples both give red flames. One is crimson and the other is orange-red. Identify the metal ions.
workedExamples.answer: Crimson: lithium ions (Li⁺); orange-red: calcium ions (Ca²⁺).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often give potassium's flame colour as purple or violet, or lithium's as just 'red'.
misconceptions.right: In fact AQA uses lilac for potassium and crimson for lithium; calcium is orange-red. Use these exact terms.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a flame test identifies the whole compound.
misconceptions.right: In fact it identifies only the metal ion; the negative ion needs a separate test.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a mixture of ions shows all the colours clearly.
misconceptions.right: In fact some colours are masked; the bright yellow of sodium can hide the lilac of potassium.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often use a yellow (safety) flame for the test.
misconceptions.right: In fact a blue (roaring) flame is used because the yellow flame has its own colour, which would hide the result.

realWorld: Fireworks use metal compounds to make colours: strontium and lithium salts for red, sodium for yellow, copper for green and blue.
Older street lamps containing sodium give out a strong yellow light.
Flame tests are a quick first check in analysing unknown salts, before more accurate instrumental methods are used.
separateOnlyContent: Flame tests and the five flame colours (Li⁺ crimson, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Cu²⁺ green) are in separate Chemistry only (8462), not Combined Science.
examTips: Learn the exact AQA colour words: crimson, yellow, lilac, orange-red, green.
Mention cleaning the wire loop in hydrochloric acid and using a blue flame in method questions.
If a question describes a mixture, consider masking: sodium yellow hides other colours.
Flame tests are part of required practical 7, so be ready to describe the method step by step.
summary: Flame tests identify metal ions by flame colour.
Li⁺ crimson, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Cu²⁺ green.
Use a clean nichrome loop and a blue Bunsen flame.
Flame tests identify only the positive ion.

questions.question: What flame colour do potassium ions produce?
markScheme: 1 mark: Lilac
questions.explanation: Potassium gives lilac. Yellow is sodium, crimson is lithium and green is copper.

questions.question: Which metal ion gives a yellow flame?
markScheme: 1 mark: Sodium
questions.explanation: Sodium ions give a strong yellow flame.

questions.question: Which metal ion gives a crimson flame?
markScheme: 1 mark: Lithium
questions.explanation: Lithium gives crimson. Calcium is orange-red, which is a different shade.

questions.question: What flame colour do copper(II) ions produce?
markScheme: 1 mark: Green
questions.explanation: Copper(II) compounds give a green flame.

questions.question: What flame colour do calcium ions produce?
markScheme: 1 mark: Orange-red
questions.explanation: Calcium gives orange-red; crimson is lithium. Students often confuse these two red colours.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the apparatus used for a flame test.
Why is the wire loop dipped in hydrochloric acid and heated in the flame before each test?
options: To make the sample stick better by melting it
To react with the metal ion
To clean it so that traces of previous samples do not affect the colour
markScheme: 1 mark: To clean it so that traces of previous samples do not affect the colour
questions.explanation: Cleaning removes contamination; otherwise a previous sample could colour the flame.

questions.question: Why is a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame used for flame tests?
options: It is hot and has almost no colour of its own
It is yellow, which makes colours brighter
markScheme: 1 mark: It is hot and has almost no colour of its own
questions.explanation: A yellow safety flame has its own colour that would confuse the result. The blue flame is hotter and nearly colourless.

questions.question: A solid contains both sodium ions and potassium ions. What is the most likely result of a flame test?
options: Separate yellow and lilac flames side by side
markScheme: 1 mark: Yellow, which masks the lilac
questions.explanation: Sodium's intense yellow masks the lilac of potassium, so the flame appears yellow.

questions.question: Which pair of compounds could NOT be distinguished from each other using only a flame test?
markScheme: 1 mark: Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate
questions.explanation: Both contain potassium ions, so both give lilac. Flame tests identify only the metal ion.

questions.question:
A student tested a solid.
Table 1 shows the results.
Which compound could the solid be?
markScheme: 1 mark: Calcium carbonate
questions.explanation: Orange-red is calcium. Copper carbonate would also be green, not white.

questions.question: Give the flame colours of lithium ions and sodium ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: lithium: crimson
1 mark: sodium: yellow
questions.explanation: These are the AQA terms; 'red' alone is not enough for lithium.

questions.question: Name the metal ion that gives a lilac flame.
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium (K⁺)
questions.explanation: Lilac is the AQA description for potassium.

questions.question: Describe how to carry out a flame test on a solid sample.
markScheme: 1 mark: clean a nichrome/platinum wire loop by dipping in (dilute) hydrochloric acid and heating in the flame
1 mark: dip the loop in the solid sample
1 mark: hold in a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame and observe the colour
questions.explanation: This is the method in required practical 7.

questions.question: Explain why flame tests cannot be used to identify all the metal ions in a mixture.
markScheme: 1 mark: some flame colours are masked/hidden by others
1 mark: for example sodium's yellow hides potassium's lilac
questions.explanation: The AQA specification states that mixtures of ions can mask some flame colours.

questions.question: A student tests copper chloride and then lithium chloride without cleaning the loop. Suggest what the student might see for the lithium chloride and why.
markScheme: 1 mark: a mixture of colours / green tinge with crimson
1 mark: copper compound left on the loop contaminates the second test
questions.explanation: Cleaning between tests prevents cross-contamination.

questions.question: A student has two white powders: lithium carbonate and calcium carbonate. Explain how a flame test could distinguish them and why care is needed with the observation.
markScheme: 1 mark: lithium gives crimson; calcium gives orange-red
1 mark: both are red shades, so compare carefully / use known reference samples side by side
questions.explanation: Using known samples for comparison helps tell similar flame colours apart.

questions.question: State the flame colour of calcium ions.
markScheme: 1 mark: orange-red
questions.explanation: Calcium's flame is orange-red, which is different from lithium's crimson.

questions.question: A sample gives no colour in a flame test. Suggest why this does not mean that the sample contains no metal ions.
acceptedAnswers: some metal ions give no colour
markScheme: 1 mark: some metal ions (for example magnesium or aluminium) do not give a characteristic flame colour
1 mark: another test, such as adding sodium hydroxide solution, is needed
questions.explanation: Only some metal ions give distinctive flame colours.

questions.question: A technician has four unlabelled white solids: lithium chloride, sodium chloride, potassium chloride and calcium chloride. Describe how flame tests could be used to identify each solid.
markScheme: Indicative content: clean nichrome loop in dilute HCl and heat until no colour
Dip loop in a small amount of the first solid
Hold in a blue Bunsen flame and observe
Clean loop between each sample
Lithium: crimson
Sodium: yellow
Potassium: lilac
Calcium: orange-red
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): method with cleaning and blue flame, and all four colours correct
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some colours correct or partial method
questions.explanation: All four compounds are chlorides, so only the metal ion differs and flame tests are ideal.

questions.question:
Required practical 7: a student carries out flame tests on three unknown solids, X, Y and Z.
Table 1 shows the results.
Identify the metal ion in each solid, describe how the student should have carried out the tests to get valid results, and evaluate the limitations of flame tests in identifying ions.
markScheme: Indicative content: X lithium (Li⁺), Y sodium (Na⁺), Z copper(II) (Cu²⁺)
Method: clean nichrome wire loop in dilute HCl and heat until no colour
Dip loop in sample; hold in edge of a blue/roaring flame
Clean between samples to avoid contamination
Compare with known reference samples
Limitation: colours in mixtures can be masked, for example sodium masks potassium
Limitation: traces of sodium contamination can give a yellow tinge, so Y could be a false result
Limitation: does not identify the negative ion; further tests (carbonates, halides, sulfates) needed
Limitation: some colours are similar (crimson and orange-red); colour judgement is subjective
Some metal ions give no flame colour
Flame emission spectroscopy is more accurate and can be used for mixtures
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three ions correct, detailed valid method and a balanced evaluation of several limitations
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): ions mostly correct with some method or limitations
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two ions identified or simple method point
questions.explanation: Top answers identify all three ions, give a careful method and evaluate the limits of the test, possibly noting instrumental alternatives.

questions.question: Which observation would show a copper(II) compound in a flame test?
markScheme: 1 mark: Green flame
questions.explanation: Copper(II) ions give a green flame.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the apparatus used for a flame test.
Which piece of equipment, labelled A, holds the sample in the flame?
markScheme: 1 mark: A nichrome wire loop
questions.explanation: A clean nichrome wire loop holds the sample in the flame.

questions.question:
A student carried out a flame test on a pure potassium compound.
Table 1 shows the expected result and the student's result.
What is the most likely cause of the student's result?
options: The loop or sample was contaminated with sodium
The sample was not heated for long enough
markScheme: 1 mark: The loop or sample was contaminated with sodium
questions.explanation: Sodium contamination is very common and its yellow masks potassium's lilac.

questions.question:
Compound Q contains one metal ion.
Table 1 shows the results of tests on compound Q.
Name compound Q.
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium (from lilac flame)
1 mark: carbonate (CO₂ with acid), so potassium carbonate
questions.explanation: Combining the flame test (metal ion) with the carbonate test (negative ion) identifies the compound.

questions.question: Which statement about flame tests is correct?
options: They identify both the positive and negative ions
They can identify every metal ion
A yellow safety flame gives the clearest results
They work best when the sample contains a single metal ion
markScheme: 1 mark: They work best when the sample contains a single metal ion
questions.explanation: Mixtures can mask colours, so single-ion samples give the most reliable results.

questions.question: A firework maker wants a firework that gives a green colour and another that gives a crimson colour. Suggest a metal compound for each.
markScheme: 1 mark: green: a copper(II) compound, for example copper chloride
1 mark: crimson: a lithium compound, for example lithium carbonate
questions.explanation: The colour depends on the metal ion, so any compound of the right metal is acceptable.
